AFD  /  Atelier for Fashion Discovery

Describe the occasion.
Get three coordinated looks, and change anything you want.

AFD is a maison that doesn’t exist. The problem it solves, getting dressed for the occasion without the catalogue, is real.

A conversational way to shop for people who already know the occasion, the mood, the weather, and the budget, but not which product names to type into a search box. It hands back complete outfits, says why each piece is there, and leaves every call up to the shopper.

Overview Problem Research Decisions Prototype Measurement Next steps

01 Overview

The idea, in one line: describe the occasion, get the whole outfit

AFD, short for Atelier for Fashion Discovery, is a fashion house I made up for this case study. The shopper I kept picturing already has the hard part figured out. It is a rooftop birthday in October, they want to look pulled together but not overdressed, they have about $400, and they are not doing yellow. What they do not have is the thing the site keeps asking for: exact product names and the right filter values. So in this concept they just say the situation, and get back three complete outfits with a plain line on why each piece is in there. From there they can swap anything, save a look, or drop the whole outfit in the bag.

What actually exists is an interactive prototype on a made-up 40-item catalogue. The engine under it is plain rules, not an LLM, and that was on purpose. I wanted the case study to test whether the experience is any good, not whether a model is.

  • North-star metric. Qualified outfit add-to-bag rate: a full look added that is in budget, in the shopper’s size, and in stock.
  • MVP. Preference intake, then three explained outfits, then swap a piece, save, and add the look to a bag.
  • Status. Concept and prototype. No user research yet. Usability testing is the next thing.

02 Problem

The gap between what a shopper knows and what the site asks for

Watch someone shop for an event and the pattern is pretty consistent. They come in with a lot already decided: the occasion, the impression they are going for, the weather, colours they love and colours they will not touch, a number in their head for the whole outfit. Then the site asks them to turn all of that into category names and filter checkboxes, and to build the outfit themselves one product page at a time. It is slow, it is fiddly, and plenty of people give up before they have put anything together.

What the shopper brings

  • The occasion and the impression they want to make
  • Weather and season
  • Size, and colours they love or avoid
  • A budget for the whole outfit

What the site asks for

  • A product category or the exact product name
  • Filter values they may not know to set
  • Coordinating separate items by hand
  • Checking budget, size, and stock over and over

This person has taste and a point of view. They shop around a specific trigger, a wedding, a new season, a trip, and they want it done quickly, but not so quickly that they end up in something that isn’t “them.”

“When I’ve got an occasion coming up, help me pull together an outfit fast, without taking away my say in how I look.”

03 Research

What I’d want to learn before building further

I have not run interviews yet. The plan is five to eight conversations with people who shop online for events, walking through one recent purchase: do they start from a product or a vibe, how do they build a full look today, what makes them trust a recommendation or ignore it, and where do budget, size, weather, and stock actually change the decision.

Usability testing plan

My next step is testing the prototype with five to eight online fashion shoppers, with diverse interests. I want to focus on whether the users can create a relevant look, understand the flow of why each item was recommended, replace unwanted pieces, and distinguish saving a look from adding it to their bag.

04 Product decisions

The calls that shaped the prototype

  • Three coordinated outfits, not a feed of items. The job is a look; three options are enough to compare without infinite scroll.
  • Every piece explained and swappable. The system proposes; the shopper decides. Keeping control of taste is the point.
  • Deterministic rules, not an LLM. It isolates the UX question, is reproducible across test sessions, runs offline for free, and becomes the baseline a probabilistic engine would later have to beat.
  • Structured intake, not free text (yet). It is the fastest path to a testable flow; parsing free-text intent into constraints is a later step.
  • Budget, size, and stock are hard limits. A look the shopper can’t actually buy is not a recommendation.

Out of scope for now: payments, accounts, real inventory, cross-session personalisation, and visual search.

05 Prototype

How the prototype builds a look

  1. Filter. Drop anything that fails a hard constraint: occasion, in stock, in the shopper’s size, not an avoided colour, weather-appropriate, under budget.
  2. Score. Rank what is left by aesthetic match, preferred or neutral colour, dress-code fit, weather fit, and budget headroom.
  3. Assemble. Greedily fill outfit slots (a dress, or a top and bottom, plus layer, shoes, bag, accessory) with a colour-harmony check, into three looks: closest match, a little bolder, and a wildcard.
  4. Explain. Build each item’s reason and the look’s total from the attributes that matched.

Same inputs always produce the same three looks, which keeps usability sessions comparable. Full logic, with a worked example, is in docs/recommendation-logic.md.

06 Measurement

How I’d know it’s working

Qualified outfit add-to-bag rate. The share of sessions where the shopper adds a complete look that is in budget, in their size, and in stock. It ties the metric to the promise: a coordinated look you can actually buy.

Supporting signals

  • Outfit completion rate
  • Time to first look
  • Recommendation-relevance rating (1 to 5)
  • Customer trust rating (1 to 5)

Guardrails

  • Irrelevant recommendations
  • Out-of-stock or over-budget items shown
  • Size-availability violations
  • Empty or partial results

Targets stay unset until there is a measured baseline. The comparison worth running is conventional category browsing versus this conversational flow, with qualified add-to-bag rate as the primary metric.

07 Next steps

Where I’d take this next

The immediate work is the usability round: 5 to 8 sessions with online fashion shoppers, plus the short interview set scoped in Research. I want to know whether people can get to a look they would actually wear, whether the per item reasons land, and whether Replace and Save read as two different actions. That is next sprint, and I am aiming to have it run and synthesized by October 24, 2026.

After that I want to make the case study quantitative. I would build a hypothetical AFD dataset (catalogue size, occasion mix, traffic, a baseline browse to bag rate) so I can model the business impact of the flow and give the A/B proposal real numbers to move against. Alongside it I would run the smaller prototype experiments already on the list: intake as a single form versus stepped, two looks versus three, explanations on versus off. The goal is to close the cycle with a go, iterate, or stop recommendation by the end of December 2026.

AFD (Atelier for Fashion Discovery) is a fictional fashion house created for this independent portfolio case study. It is not a real company and is not affiliated with any real brand. All products, prices, materials, inventory, and recommendations are invented to demonstrate the concept.
